newsitem.title: USA: U.S. FDA to weigh risk of BSE diseases and gelatin.
newsitem.headline: U.S. FDA to weigh risk of BSE diseases and gelatin.

text.p: A Food and Drug Administration panel will meet Wednesday and Thursday to make recommendations on how to reduce the risk to humans of mad cow disease and similar animal diseases from gelatin products.

There has been no evidence that the animal diseases known as transmissible spongiform encephalopathies (TSEs) are present in gelatin, but the agency wants to address any potential risk as soon as possible, an FDA spokesman said.

Gelatin is produced from boiled animal bones and hooves and is used in a wide variety of products regulated by the FDA, including pharmaceutical capsules, vaccines, cosmetics, dietary supplements, candies, medical devices, and foods.

The FDA advisory committee will be briefed on the gelatin manufacturing process and whether it can safely remove the threat of TSE contamination. The panel will also hear from TSE experts and industry representatives.
Concern about TSEs and their potential to infect humans through ingestion of infected animal products has grown in the last few years.

In March 1996, the British government said it had evidence of a new variant of Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease. The government said that the 10 people with the new form may have gotten it from eating meat from cows infected with bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), or mad cow disease, a form of TSE.
In January, the FDA issued a proposal to ban ruminant byproducts from being fed to ruminants, a practice believed to have spread BSE in Britain.
The agency recently issued a draft rule expanding that proposal to ban all animal protein from ruminant feed, and said it would accept public comments until April 28.
